about.en:
IBSU's American Studies training, billed as 'a chance to travel to America', introduces school pupils to the United States: its global influence, history and culture, everyday modern American life, and relations between the US and Georgia.

The sessions are run on the IBSU campus in Tbilisi by successful students of the university's American Studies programme, and mix short talks with themed, game-style activities so participants apply what they learn. The registration form accepts pupils in grades 9 to 12.

It is a light, low-pressure way to test an interest in international relations, American culture or English-language study before choosing a university programme.

en: Introduction to US history, culture and society
Led by IBSU American Studies students
Interactive themed activities on campus

about.en:
Business Alphabet (ბიზნეს ანბანი) is a free student-run project of the IBSU Business School that aims to deepen school pupils' understanding of business. Participants get short introductions to marketing, finance, accounting, management and tourism.

The trainings are prepared and delivered by IBSU business students on the university campus in Tbilisi. The project has run since 2014 and, according to IBSU, more than 5,000 pupils have taken part. It is aimed at pupils in grades 10, 11 and 12.

It is a good first step for anyone considering business, economics or tourism at university, and a useful line for a CV or application.

en: Free since 2014, 5,000+ past participants

about.en:
IBSU's Journalism for School Students is a free training covering four topics: journalism as a profession, journalism ethics, preparing a news story, and methods for verifying information.

Alongside the sessions, participants take part in practical activities and learn to use IBSU's own television and radio facilities on the Tbilisi campus. The training is open to pupils in grades 9 to 12.

It suits students who write for a school paper, run social media, or are thinking about media, communications or political science at university.

about.en:
Ask the Psychologist (ჰკითხე ფსიქოლოგს) is a free IBSU project for pupils in grades 10, 11 and 12. It is led by Teona Guburiani, head of IBSU's psychology programme, together with successful psychology students.

The session starts with fun group activities and continues with an open discussion in which pupils ask questions on topics that interest them and get detailed answers. It takes place on the IBSU campus in Tbilisi and is run in Georgian.

It is a relaxed introduction to psychology as a subject and a career, useful for students weighing up social-science degrees.

about.en:
The Art of Negotiation (მოლაპარაკების ხელოვნება) is a school-pupil training led by IBSU lecturer Davit Bragvadze, who draws on years of experience in conflict management.

The first part covers proven rules and methods of problem solving, techniques used by diplomats, and etiquette and professional standards. The second part includes a themed film screening, a discussion and other activities. The registration form accepts pupils in grades 9 to 12; sessions are held on the IBSU campus in Tbilisi in Georgian.

It pairs well with Model UN and debate: students learn how real negotiators prepare, frame and close a deal.

Diplomatic negotiation techniques and etiquette
Film screening and discussion

about.en:
State Organisation (სახელმწიფო მოწყობა) is a free IBSU project for pupils in grades 10, 11 and 12. Participants learn the main characteristics of a state, state symbols, forms and systems of government, the separation of powers, economic organisation, local self-government and international relations.

They then apply this in practical, game-like tasks, including creating their own states. The project is led by lecturer Ana Gogoladze with IBSU International Relations students and runs in Georgian on the Tbilisi campus.

Useful preparation for civics olympiads, Model UN and law or political-science degrees.

Geopolitical Games (გეოპოლიტიკური თამაშები) is a free IBSU project that combines theory with a practical competition. The practical part is a themed competition held in the university grounds. The project is led by Nino Samkharadze, lecturer in IBSU's International Relations programme, with IR students; it is aimed at pupils in grades 10-12 and runs in Georgian in Tbilisi.

Ideal for students drawn to MUN, diplomacy or IR degrees who want a competitive, hands-on introduction.

The training is free, runs in Georgian on the IBSU campus in Tbilisi and is coordinated by IBSU students.

The skills transfer directly to school clubs, volunteering, startup competitions and university applications that ask for evidence of initiative.

about.en:
The Bachelor's Student Grant (BSG) competition is run by the Shota Rustaveli National Science Foundation of Georgia to support students' scientific interests, innovative ideas and research skills, and their involvement in education and science popularisation. Each project can request up to 15,000 GEL.

A project needs a project leader and at least three main personnel, who must be Georgian citizens and active students on an accredited bachelor's programme at a Georgian higher-education institution. They apply through a lead organisation: a Georgian university, a public-law entity or a registered Georgian non-profit. Projects are registered in the Foundation's GMUS system between 30 October and 13 November 2026 (18:00), and the signed participation application goes to the Foundation by 17 November 2026. Online consultations are held on 3 and 10 November at 16:00; results and grant agreements are due in December 2026.

For undergraduates this is a rare chance to lead a funded research project of their own, which carries real weight in master's and PhD applications.

about.en:
The Leonardo da Vinci competition (LEO) is the Shota Rustaveli National Science Foundation's annual contest for school inventors and young researchers. Its aim is to encourage pupils' interest in learning, innovation and technology and to build creative thinking and practical skills.

Pupils in grades 7-12 at any Georgian state or private school can enter alone or in a group of up to three. In stage 1 (registration in spring, through the Foundation's GMUS system) they submit an initial idea or research plan; selected projects go to stage 2 (autumn), where they submit a full description and a physical drawing, model or mock-up. Finalists present at an exhibition in November-December, where winners are chosen and prize money is paid. In 2026 the call opened on 10 March with stage-1 registration from 16 March to 24 April; expect a similar timetable in 2027.

It is the main national science-fair-style competition for Georgian pupils and a strong addition to any STEM university application.

This European Solidarity Corps Humanitarian Aid placement with Association Merkuri in Zugdidi (western Georgia) suits someone interested in community engagement, climate resilience and disaster preparedness. The volunteer helps communities understand environmental risks and prepare for floods and extreme weather by organising workshops, discussions, awareness events and small community initiatives, preparing materials and collecting feedback, working closely with active residents and especially women.

The placement runs from 4 January to 3 July 2027 as part of the RISE project, with language classes, intercultural activities, three-way mentoring and pre-departure training. Accommodation is with a host family (private room), plus a monthly allowance; travel, visa and insurance are covered.

Courses are online, in Georgian, usually in the evenings, last three to six months and take about 20-30 students each. Graduates get a certificate and the strongest may be offered jobs at TBC and its subsidiaries. TBC states that registration for most courses opens in the autumn; the current intake is closed.

It encourages research, experiments, inventions, engineering models and prototypes, and builds research, public-speaking and presentation skills. The 2026 theme was 'The Digital Era and Its Challenges'.

Sections cover linguistics and literature, mathematics, history, geography, chemistry, biology, physics, programming and modern technologies, engineering and architecture, and civic education. A free, nationwide platform for a first research project, useful for olympiad-minded pupils and for university applications.

It is individual and open to pupils in grades 9-12. about.en:
Lavoisier Circle (ლავუაზიეს წრე) is a team competition for pupils fascinated by biology, chemistry and the molecular make-up of living things, organised jointly by the Agricultural University of Georgia and Free University of Tbilisi.

Teams have up to three members, at least two of them final-year applicants; teammates can come from different schools, and individuals can register and be matched with a team. No prior preparation is required. In 2026 the two rounds were held at the Kakha Bendukidze Campus on 3 and 15 March. The top three teams win tuition grants of 15,000, 9,000 and 4,500 GEL (split equally between members) for bachelor's study in agronomy, natural sciences and biotechnology, veterinary medicine or engineering at the Agricultural University, or physics at Free University.

Generous prizes and a hands-on format make it one of the most rewarding school science contests in Georgia.
